name: Shona religion (Mwari/mhondoro/vadzimu)

dating.dating_summary: The Mwari cult's documented, source-rich history begins with its 17th-18th century Rozvi (Changamire dynasty) association and Matopos/Njelele shrine geography; its presence at Great Zimbabwe specifically (13th-15th c.) during the site's floruit is an inference/extrapolation backward from later evidence, not independently evidenced from the site's own archaeological record — report as contested, not settled.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: No archaeological dating specific to the Njelele shrine site (as distinct from general Matopos-region settlement) was located in this research pass.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Portuguese-era sources document Mwari as the Mutapa state's tutelary/creator deity from the 16th-17th century (referenced via Portuguese missionary accounts, e.g. Dom Gonçalo da Silveira's 1570 mission); an exact earliest-dated primary citation using the specific term "Mwari" was not independently verified in this pass.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: Terence Ranger, Revolt in Southern Rhodesia 1896-97 (Heinemann, 1967); M.L. Daneel, The God of the Matopo Hills: An Essay on the Mwari Cult in Rhodesia (Mouton, 1970), based on 1965-67 fieldwork — the foundational modern academic study.

tradition_internal_claim.note: Some oral accounts place cult origin around a 14th-century "Mbire" migration narrative of Karanga clans from the Lake regions — self-reported, not independently corroborated.

notes: DISPUTED relationship to Great Zimbabwe/Rozvi state power: Camp 1 (some earlier/popular accounts + the Mbire migration tradition) treats the cult as continuous with or originating at Great Zimbabwe; Innocent Pikirayi (The Zimbabwe Culture, AltaMira Press, 2001) cautions against reading the cult as a mere instrument of state power even in its later Rozvi-era form; David Beach argued documentary/oral linkage between the archaeological site and the cult during the site's 13th-15th c. floruit is weak; Richard Werbner (Kalanga fieldwork) argues the cult historically never was structurally bound to any specific state/polity at all. mhondoro (territorial ancestral spirits, ranked above vadzimu/ordinary family ancestors) mediate between Mwari and the living; see claim_nehanda_does_not_demonstrate for the 1896-97 First Chimurenga case.
